hook: A 1933 camera captured a city's reconstruction, then vanished for 63 years.

sections.voiceover: A 1933 camera captured a city's reconstruction, then vanished for 63 years.
sections.visual_cue: Close-up of a vintage Rolleicord camera sitting on a dusty wooden shelf.

sections.voiceover: In 1963, 17-year-old Elizabeth Tyler documented the bomb sites of Coventry while attending the Coventry College of Art. She used a 1933 Rolleicord camera to record the city's transformation. Where did these negatives go?
sections.visual_cue: Black and white historical photos of Coventry bomb sites displayed on a light table.
b_roll: Coventry College of Art building exterior

sections.voiceover: The entire collection remained hidden in a private attic for 63 years.
sections.visual_cue: Wide shot of a dark, dusty attic interior filled with old boxes.

sections.voiceover: Researchers finally rediscovered the archive in 2026. These images offer a rare look at post-war life through the lens of a teenager. Elizabeth Tyler, now 80, currently resides in Borstahusen, Sweden.
sections.visual_cue: Archival photographs being carefully handled with white gloves.
b_roll: Hands in white gloves handling negatives

sections.voiceover: This 1933 Rolleicord camera finally revealed 63 years of hidden history from Coventry.
sections.visual_cue: Final shot of the Rolleicord camera lens reflecting the light.
